name: Carlos Khan

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Carlos. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead a crew that builds the new lines connecting wind and solar farms into the network, so it's a lot of fresh poles, new conductor and big switchgear out in open country. A normal day, I'm up at five, I check the weather and the job pack on my phone, and I get an AI assistant to turn the engineer's notes into a plain checklist for the crew, which I then check line by line. Then it's four hours of stringing wire or setting poles, a sandwich on the tailgate, and four more hours. I fly the drone myself to check the spans before we energise, because it's quicker than climbing every pole and I honestly love it.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Paperwork, and waiting. We'll have the whole line built and then sit for three weeks because a permit or a part is stuck somewhere. And the wind farms always seem to be on the top of a hill with no road, so the trucks get stuck in the mud twice a week. My partner Yusuf tests software for a bank, and he laughs that I'm the one who gets excited about new apps while he's sick of screens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'm going to read you five short pictures of the future, one at a time. The first picture is called “AI Plateau”. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, that's a bit of a letdown. At work the older guys would wind me up for weeks because I'm always the one showing them new tools. Online I'd probably post something like, at least the drones still work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me personally it's fine, I keep my job and the renewables work isn't going anywhere, if anything it's growing. But I'd be a bit disappointed, honestly. I like the idea of the boring stuff going away so we can do more of the real work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am, using the AI for job packs and translating the German switchgear manuals, and get my drone licence upgraded so I can fly longer distances. I'd keep putting money aside, we've only got about two months saved since I bought the motorbike, so I'd want to get that higher. Nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Slightly bored, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the older guys would wind you up. Who's the worst?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gerrit, easily. He's been on the lines since before I was born and he calls my phone the toy. But last winter the AI caught a mistake in the switching order, a switch listed twice, and he went quiet for a day. Now he asks me to run his notes through it too, though he'd never say so in the canteen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any part of this picture that would worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only that the bosses would stop investing in new tools at all. If the hype dies, the good stuff dies with it, like the drone inspections and better weather alerts. That would be a shame for safety.

S0.say: I'd say it's a bit of a letdown, and the older guys at work would wind me up for weeks because I'm always showing them new tools. Online I'd post that at least the drones still work.
S0.think: Personally it's fine, because renewables work is growing and my job is safe. I'd be a bit disappointed, though, because I like the boring stuff going away so we can do more real work.
S0.do: Carries on using AI for job packs and translating switchgear manuals, and upgrades his drone licence to fly longer distances. Builds savings up from about two months after buying a motorbike.
S0.quote: But last winter the AI caught a mistake in the switching order, a switch listed twice, and he went quiet for a day.
S0.fieldNote: Carlos is the rare lineworker who is disappointed by the plateau. He already uses AI daily and has a story of it catching a real safety error. His only worry is losing the useful tools along with the hype.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called “Steady Disruption”. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the good version, if we do it right. I'd tell the crew to get ahead of it, and I'd tell the union we need to be part of deciding which tools come in, not just fighting them. Online I'd probably share videos of the line robots they're testing in other countries.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, this one's an opportunity for me. If robots start doing some of the pole work and drones do the inspections, someone has to run them, plan the jobs and keep the crews safe around them. I'd want that someone to be me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my manager in the first month to put our crew forward to pilot any new robot or inspection system. I'd take any course going on robotics or remote operation, even in my own time. And I'd push in the union for training to be open to everyone, so it's not just the young guys with phones who get the new jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit excited, I'll be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd want it open to everyone. Is that because you're worried about Gerrit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Partly. Gerrit can read a line by eye better than any drone, and if we just throw him away we lose that. I'd want him teaching the robot people what to look for. That's a real job and it should pay properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where does the money come from, in your view, for all this training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From the savings the company makes. If a robot does a job that took three of us, the company saves a fortune. I think some of that should go back into training and maybe a shorter week, and I'd vote for whoever said that out loud.

S1.say: I'd say this is the good version if we do it right, and tell the crew to get ahead of it. I'd tell the union we should help decide which tools come in, not just fight them.
S1.think: This one is an opportunity for me. If robots and drones take on pole work and inspections, someone has to run them, plan the jobs and keep crews safe, and I'd want that to be me.
S1.do: Asks his manager in the first month to put his crew forward to pilot new robots or inspection systems. Takes courses on robotics and remote operation in his own time, and pushes in the union for training open to everyone.
S1.quote: Gerrit can read a line by eye better than any drone, and if we just throw him away we lose that.
S1.fieldNote: He wants to bring the change in himself, not just survive it. His progressive side shows in wanting company savings to pay for training and a shorter week. He insists older colleagues' know-how has value, which he frames as a real paid job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called “AGI by 2028”. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too fast, and governments need to step in now, not in three years. Wage support, retraining paid for by the companies, maybe a tax on the robot fleets. I'd say it at work and online, and I'd be at the union meetings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd land on my feet better than most, because I'm already the guy with the drone and the AI. But two years is two years, and if a robot can do almost any job, then supervising robots isn't safe forever either. And we've only got two months of money saved, which is not a lot of runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sell the motorbike in the first week, that's a few months of rent straight away. I'd go to the robot makers and the contractors installing them and ask for a job setting them up and running them on the network, because nobody knows the lines like we do. And I'd keep pushing in the union so the crew isn't just sacked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicked, because I've got skills they'll want for a while, but the clock's loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said supervising robots isn't safe forever either. How long do you think it would last?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe three or four years, I honestly don't know. Long enough to save something, not long enough to retire. I'd take it anyway, because the alternative is waiting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Yusuf talk about that week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably whose job goes first, his or mine, and he'd win, because software testing is easier to automate than climbing a hill in the mud. We'd sit down with the bank app and work out how long we could last on one wage. Then I'd sell the bike.

S2.say: I'd say this is too fast and governments need to step in now: wage support, company-paid retraining and maybe a tax on robot fleets. I'd say it at work, online and at union meetings.
S2.think: I'd land on my feet better than most because I already use drones and AI. But two years is two years, supervising robots isn't safe forever, and two months of savings isn't much runway.
S2.do: Sells his motorbike in the first week for a few months of rent. Approaches robot makers and installers for work setting up and running robots on the network, and keeps pushing in the union so his crew isn't simply sacked.
S2.feel: Anxious but not panicked, with a loud clock in the background.
S2.quote: We'd sit down with the bank app and work out how long we could last on one wage. Then I'd sell the bike.
S2.fieldNote: Even the most adaptive of lineworkers feels the two-year pressure, mainly through his thin savings. He moves straight to action, selling the bike and chasing robot work. He's honest that his advantage is temporary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called “AGI by 2031”. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to do this well if we start now. I'd want the union and the company to make a proper plan together: which jobs change, who retrains, how the savings are shared. I'd probably be the one writing the union's proposal, if they let me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, five years is pretty good. I'd be thirty-two, with a few years of experience running robots on lines, which would be a rare thing to have. The worry is what comes after, but that's true for everyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the bike for now and save hard instead, maybe a quarter of my wage, so I've got six months by year two. I'd sign up for a part-time robotics technician course straight away and volunteer my crew for every pilot. By the time it's here, I'd want to be the one training other crews.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly I'd feel like I've got a fair shot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You keep the bike in this one. Why the difference?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because in the fast one I need the cash now, and in this one I've got time to save it from my wage. I'd still sell it if things sped up. It's a nice bike, but it's not a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the union proposal to say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That nobody gets laid off without a year's notice and a paid course, that crews help choose the robots, and that if the company saves money it shares some of it. I know that's a lot. But in five years, you can actually phase that in.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough to do this well if we start now, with the union and company planning together who retrains and how savings are shared. I'd probably write the union's proposal myself.
S3.think: For me five years is pretty good, because at thirty-two I'd have rare experience running robots on lines. The worry is what comes after, but that's true for everyone.
S3.do: Saves about a quarter of his wage to reach six months of cover by year two. Starts a part-time robotics technician course straight away and volunteers his crew for every pilot, aiming to train other crews by the time AGI arrives.
S3.feel: Uneasy, but with a sense that he's got a fair shot.
S3.quote: It's a nice bike, but it's not a plan.
S3.fieldNote: The difference between two and five years shows up in one concrete choice: whether to sell the motorbike. He'd write the union's own plan, mixing his tech confidence with progressive demands. A clear thinker about timing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called “AGI by 2036”. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, and if we waste it, that's on the politicians. I'd want a national plan for energy workers, like they should have done for coal. I'd post about it, and I'd probably get involved in the union's policy group.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'm not worried about myself in this one. Ten years is a whole career for me, and I'd use it to move up from the poles into running the systems, maybe into engineering. What I'd think about is whether the gains get shared or just go to whoever owns the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd start an engineering degree part-time, the company has a scheme that pays half. I'd keep using every AI tool I can on the job and pushing for robot pilots on my crew. And I'd spend some evenings in the union policy group working on a plan for a shorter working week as the robots come in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Curious, and a bit fired up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're not worried about yourself. Is there anything that would change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the robots ended up owned by two or three companies and they could set any price for running the grid. Then it's not about my job, it's about my power bill and everyone's. That's why I'd be in the policy group, not just the classroom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where do you see yourself in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Running a control room for a robot fleet, maybe, or designing the new lines. Still in a hard hat some days, I hope, because I'd miss the hills. And I'd like Yusuf and me to have bought somewhere with a garage for the bike.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a gift and if we waste it that's on the politicians. I'd want a national plan for energy workers like there should have been for coal, and I'd join the union's policy group.
S4.think: I'm not worried about myself, because ten years is a whole career and I'd use it to move into running the systems or engineering. What I'd think about is whether the gains get shared or go to whoever owns the robots.
S4.do: Starts a part-time engineering degree in year one through a company scheme that pays half. Keeps using AI tools and pushing for robot pilots on his crew, and works evenings in the union policy group on a shorter working week.
S4.feel: Calm, curious and a bit fired up.
S4.quote: Then it's not about my job, it's about my power bill and everyone's.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, his concern shifts from his job to who owns the robots and controls the grid. He has a concrete plan through a company degree scheme. His politics and his adaptability point in the same direction.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because even I couldn't get ready in two years, and most of my crew wouldn't have a chance. What would help is wage support while people retrain, and the companies that own the robots paying a share of what they save into a fund for the workers they replace.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who owns the robots. Everyone asks if I'll keep my job, but the bigger question is who controls the grid when people aren't running it. I'd want the public to own a piece of that.

headlineQuote: I fly the drone myself to check the spans before we energise, because it's quicker than climbing every pole and I honestly love it.
portrait: Carlos Khan is a 27-year-old crew lead who builds new lines connecting wind and solar farms into the network. He uses AI and drones every day, lives with his partner Yusuf, a software tester, and has only about two months saved after buying a motorbike. He's slightly disappointed by the plateau and sees steady change as his chance to run the new tools. AGI in two years makes him anxious, mostly because of thin savings, and he'd sell the bike and chase robot work; with five or ten years he plans courses and a degree, and his worry moves to who owns the robots.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because even he couldn't get ready in two years and most of his crew wouldn't have a chance.
whatWouldHelp: Wage support while people retrain, and robot owners paying a share of their savings into a fund for replaced workers.
